primary_meaning: Being made holy for God: set apart as belonging to God, cleansed from sin, and transformed toward holy conduct and Christlike character. In much Christian teaching, “sanctification” especially denotes the Holy Spirit’s continuing work of moral and spiritual renewal in believers.
primary_basis: Leviticus 20:7–8, 26 — God sanctifies his people and sets them apart as holy.
John 17:17–19 — Jesus asks the Father to sanctify his disciples in the truth.
Romans 6:19–22 — freedom from sin bears fruit leading to sanctification and eternal life.
1 Corinthians 6:11 — believers are described as washed, sanctified, and justified.
1 Thessalonians 4:3–7 — sanctification is identified with abstaining from sexual immorality and living in holiness.
1 Thessalonians 5:23–24 — Paul prays that God will sanctify believers completely.
2 Thessalonians 2:13 — sanctification is attributed to the Spirit.
Hebrews 10:10, 14 — sanctification is grounded in Christ’s once-for-all offering.
Hebrews 12:14 — believers are commanded to pursue holiness.
1 Peter 1:15–16 — God’s people are called to be holy because God is holy.

alternatives.meaning: Consecration or dedication: to sanctify is primarily to set a person, place, object, or time apart for God’s possession and service, without necessarily implying an inward moral process.
basis: Exodus 19:10–14 — the people are consecrated in preparation for meeting God.
Exodus 29:43–44 — the tabernacle, altar, and priests are sanctified.
Genesis 2:3 — God sanctifies the seventh day.
John 10:36 — the Father sanctifies and sends the Son.

alternatives.meaning: Definitive or positional sanctification: believers are sanctified once for all through union with Christ and his sacrifice, so sanctification can describe an accomplished status as well as an ongoing process.
basis: 1 Corinthians 1:2 — Christians are addressed as those already sanctified in Christ.
1 Corinthians 6:11 — sanctification is spoken of as a completed event.
Hebrews 10:10, 14 — believers have been sanctified through Christ’s offering, while also being perfected in an ongoing sense.
Acts 20:32; 26:18 — the sanctified are described as an identifiable people receiving an inheritance.

alternatives.meaning: Entire sanctification or Christian perfection: sanctification may culminate in a distinct work of grace in this life characterized by perfected love or deliverance from willful sin. This is especially associated with Wesleyan and Holiness traditions.
basis: Matthew 5:48 — the command to be perfect as the heavenly Father is perfect.
1 Thessalonians 5:23–24 — prayer for complete sanctification.
Hebrews 6:1 — exhortation to go on to perfection or maturity.
1 John 4:17–18 — perfected love casts out fear.

alternatives.meaning: Sanctification as participation in divine life or theosis: holiness is understood chiefly as transformative communion with God and participation by grace in the divine nature, particularly in Eastern Christian interpretation.
basis: 2 Peter 1:4 — believers become participants in the divine nature.
2 Corinthians 3:18 — believers are transformed into the Lord’s image from glory to glory.
John 17:21–23 — Jesus prays for the disciples’ union with God.
1 John 3:2–3 — seeing Christ is associated with becoming like him and purification.

alternatives.meaning: Sacramental sanctification: God communicates sanctifying grace especially through baptism, Eucharist, and the Church’s sacramental life. This reading is prominent in Catholic, Orthodox, and some Anglican and Lutheran traditions.
basis: Acts 2:38 — baptism is connected with forgiveness and the gift of the Holy Spirit.
Romans 6:3–4 — baptism unites believers with Christ’s death and resurrection.
1 Corinthians 10:16–17 — Eucharistic participation is communion in Christ.
Ephesians 5:25–27 — Christ cleanses and sanctifies the Church through washing with water and the word.

notes: There is broad consensus on the core meaning of holiness, belonging to God, and separation from sin. There is no single settled consensus on whether sanctification should be emphasized as an accomplished status, a lifelong process, sacramental transformation, participation in divine life, or a distinct experience of entire sanctification. In Scripture the term is not merely symbolic; it has cultic, relational, ethical, and soteriological uses.
